claims.text: Brittle behavior in an initially single-phase fcc HEA emerges through an intrinsic transition away from homogeneous activation of multiple slip systems.
The proposed deformation transition produces localized stacking faults and incipient shear bands.
Localized stacking faults and shear bands cause stress concentration and early crack nucleation.
Crack nucleation in the HEA occurs independently of grain-boundary segregation and intergranular precipitation.
The initial material is a chemically and microstructurally homogeneous, disordered, single-phase fcc HEA.
The initial HEA is suitable for high-temperature and demanding engineering service.

Temperature- and strain-rate-controlled in situ straining microscopy, with a grain-boundary-sensitive conventional alloy as a matched control, can distinguish the proposed intrinsic mechanism from a conventional grain-boundary mechanism.
Single-phase fcc HEAs and MEAs can undergo rapid ductility loss at intermediate temperatures of approximately 400–800°C.
Diffusion and thermally activated mechanisms become significant in the proposed 400–800°C regime.
Thermally induced changes in local bonding or chemical order may reduce the HEA's ability to activate multiple slip systems.
Reduced multiple-slip activity concentrates dislocations, which then form dense stacking faults and incipient shear bands.
Multiple simultaneously active deformation mechanisms can alleviate stress concentration and promote uniform plastic deformation and ductility.
Relative to room temperature, the HEA will show reduced diversity and spatial homogeneity of slip-system activation at intermediate temperatures.
Localized stacking-fault clusters and shear bands will increase and will precede crack nucleation at intermediate temperatures.
At room temperature, the HEA uniformly activates multiple slip systems and consequently has excellent ductility and toughness without localization.
The conventional-alloy control will initiate failure at grain boundaries because of segregation or precipitate-induced stress concentration.
The proposed mechanism is bounded to intermediate temperatures of approximately 400–800°C and engineering strain rates.
At very low or very high temperatures, or at extremely high strain rates, other deformation or failure mechanisms may dominate.
